name: Karl Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and still fairly new to the contact-centre billing line. I finished secondary school and do the plain calls; when a customer has two account numbers I usually ask another agent to check my answer. I am paid at the lower end. I have never used an AI tool, and I am still learning the centre’s own screens.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner June cleans offices four mornings a week, and our children are grown and live elsewhere. We have less than a month of expenses put away. There are not many similar call jobs nearby. Retirement is nearer than it used to be, but I need to know what money we actually have before I say when I can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau sounds like a small shortcut, and I would ask for the old billing guide to stay by my headset. A customer needs the right amount, even if the answer takes an extra minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre still needs people for calls, but my own pay is low and we have less than a month saved. June’s four mornings of cleaning would not cover both of us if I missed a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking basic billing calls and ask a paid-shift colleague to walk me through a disputed payment twice. In the first year of this small change, I’d leave our worn but working kettle alone instead of replacing it and keep that money for the bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even with ordinary work. A small shortcut does not put another week’s pay in our drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your colleague show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mixed up the payment date and the posting date last Tuesday. My colleague showed me both lines, and I corrected the note before the customer rang back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase would you delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: June (my partner) would use the old kettle until it fails. We are holding a little cash for work travel, not building a new investment.

say: I’d ask to keep the **billing guide** near my headset.
I’d say **correct amounts** matter more than a one-minute saving.
think: I think **basic calls** still need agents in this picture.
I worry **thin savings** and June’s part-time work cannot cover lost pay.
do: Keep **basic billing calls** and review a disputed payment with a colleague on paid time.
Delay **replacing the kettle** while it works and keep the cost for bus travel.
S0.quote: A small shortcut does not put another week’s pay in our drawer.
fieldNote: His **low wage** keeps the mild scenario financially tense.
He is **still learning** two dates on the current billing screen.
The **kettle delay** preserves bus money without claiming new savings.

steps.text: Keep taking basic billing calls and review payment dates with colleague on paid time
Delay replacing working kettle and hold its cost for bus fares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers Steady Disruption could answer the simple bills I now take. I would ask management how many paid basic-call shifts are left before choosing a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the firm may keep its experienced agents and cut the beginner rota. Less than a month saved and few nearby centres make that a serious loss, even if June keeps her cleaning hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a list of the bill types I can settle without help and ask my supervisor for written paid-hour plans. If my shifts fall in the first year routine calls move, I’d apply for a posted paid reception job only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our bills after bus fare, and keep this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possibility of a shorter week. I cannot pay the rent with an offer of training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which calls would disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count how many plain balance questions disappear, because those are my current shifts. A total call count would hide which worker lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: June (my partner) would check the morning bus times with me. A job that starts before the first bus is no job I can hold.

say: I’d request **written paid-hour plans** for beginner shifts before accepting a course offer.
I’d count **plain balance calls** moved to software.
think: I think the **beginner rota** could be cut before experienced shifts.
I fear **few local centres** and thin savings make that loss hard.
do: List **settled bill types** and ask for written paid hours in 2026.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid reception** with written after-fare bill-covering weekly wages/hours and reachable first bus; keep current wages until signing.
S1.quote: A job that starts before the first bus is no job I can hold.
fieldNote: He tracks **his own basic-call work**, not the whole queue.
A manager inquiry is **individual**, not group worker action.
A posted job needs **usable bus times** and written bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Keep settling basic bills and ask supervisor for written paid hours
Apply after cuts for posted reception with written after-fare bill-covering wages/hours and usable first bus
Keep current paid billing job until a suitable offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the floor AGI by 2028 could take the ordinary bill calls as well as the difficult ones. Robots around 2031 are later, and I work on a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior shifts could end before I am properly settled into them. Less than a month saved means June and I would feel the missing wage in the next bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for written dates of any lost shifts and look for posted paid counter work on the bus route. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d apply only for a written offer with weekly wages and hours covering our bills after the fare; I would keep current shifts until it was signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The bus pass has to be bought before a new job pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the shop what the counter worker actually does and whether the opening is paid. A friendly manager saying “come back soon” would not be a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your son bridge travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could ask our grown son Daniel whether he is able to cover one bus pass if the first wage is late. He has his own household, so I would not count that money until he agreed and I knew when to repay him.

say: I’d seek **written cut dates** for the junior rota.
I’d say **2028 AGI** reaches phone work before robots.
think: I think my **junior shifts** could end quickly.
I know **under one month saved** leaves little room for a search.
do: Seek **written shift dates** and inspect posted paid counter work on the bus route.
Apply after lost calls for **posted paid counter work** with written after-fare bill-covering weekly wages/hours; keep current shifts until signing.
Ask **son Daniel** about one bus pass only if first pay is late, with repayment agreed.
feel: **Alarmed** by an immediate wage and travel gap.
S2.quote: The bus pass has to be bought before a new job pays me.
fieldNote: His **junior phone work** is exposed by 2028.
Daniel’s help is **uncertain, capped and repayable**.
A counter job needs a **posted paid opening** and signed after-fare terms.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid counter openings along the bus route
Apply after lost calls for posted counters with written after-fare bill-covering wages/hours; keep shifts until signing
Ask son Daniel for one bus pass if first pay lags; agree repayment before accepting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to see if an office counter really has a paid vacancy. I would ask the employer for a trial with a person beside me, not a computer course at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn a different payment screen slowly if someone shows me while I still earn here. Full thinking AI could do that counter work as well, so I would need a real posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d request a supervised paid trial only if the nearby service office posts a paid counter opening. If that opening requires a records course, I’d take it only when the employer pays both the fee and study hours. In the first year after 2031 I’d move only on a signed written weekly wage and hours covering bills after bus fare, keeping my call wage until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with five years to inspect the work. I can read a new screen on a paid shift; I cannot buy a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try on the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would follow one payment from the customer’s receipt to the account line with a worker beside me. If I cannot see the correction, I would not say I know the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would June check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: June (my partner) and I would check the first bus against the counter opening time. We would not take a role that costs more to reach than it adds to our week.

say: I’d ask for a **supervised paid trial** at a posted counter opening.
I’d reject an **unpaid home course** offered instead of work.
think: I think I could learn **counter payments** with a person beside me.
I know **2031 AGI** could also handle that screen.
do: Request **supervised paid counter trial** only for a posted opening in 2026.
Take **required records course** only with employer-paid fees and study hours for that role.
Move after 2031 only with **signed after-fare bill-covering wage**, written hours and workable bus times.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a real shift.
S3.quote: I can read a new screen on a paid shift; I cannot buy a promise.
fieldNote: He needs **person-led practice** rather than home study alone.
The **posted paid opening** gates both trial and required course.
Bus time and fare decide **usable weekly pay**.

steps.text: Try supervised paid counter shift only for posted paid opening
Take required records course only for posted paid counter opening with employer-paid fees and study hours
Move on signed written after-fare bill-covering weekly wages/hours only if first bus reaches opening time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2036 gives us years to ask about wages and retirement, but it does not put cash in a worker’s pocket. I would ask for an annual written rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still be working at 68 because I have not checked what June and I could live on after work. Full thinking AI could take my calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 would not postpone that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid billing shifts and write down our weekly bills beside the actual wage and savings. If I still need a wage in the first year after 2036 and my hours fall, I’d move to posted paid counter work only on a signed offer covering bills after bus fare and with enough weekly hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about making the years add up. A long timetable is no use if I cannot afford the last year of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What money would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count money from a pension until I had checked that it exists and what it pays. I would decide whether to stop work from real figures with June, not an age on a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children support retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our adult children have expenses of their own. I would not ask them to carry our retirement unless they offered, and even then I would want a clear amount.

say: I’d ask for an **annual written rota** and real wage figures.
I’d say **older workers** may still need wages beyond 2036.
think: I think I may **work at 68** if our money is short.
I cannot assume **pension income** before checking it.
do: Keep **paid billing shifts** and compare actual wages, bills and savings in 2026.
Move if wages remain needed after cuts to **posted paid counter work**, with signed after-fare bill-covering wages and sufficient weekly hours.
S4.quote: A long timetable is no use if I cannot afford the last year of work.
fieldNote: He avoids assuming a **pension entitlement** or retirement date.
The **thin reserve** keeps even the decade scenario financially tense.
Adult children’s **support is unpromised**, not an income plan.

steps.text: Keep paid billing shifts and compare actual weekly wages, bills and savings
Move if wages remain needed after cuts to posted paid counters with signed after-fare bill-covering wages/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one that worries me. Simple billing calls are exactly what I am still learning, and less than a month saved would not support a long search. I would need written notice of any lost hours and a real nearby paid opening with enough weekly pay after the bus fare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Someone should ask a worker to show the weekly pay packet, not just their age. Being 58 does not tell you whether I can afford to retire.

headlineQuote: Being 58 does not tell you whether I can afford to retire.
portrait: At **58**, Karl is a junior billing agent still learning after secondary school.
He and June have **grown children** and less than one month of expenses saved.
His **lower wage** and few nearby call jobs make paid hours crucial.
He **never uses AI** and will not assume retirement money he has not checked.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end the simple calls he depends on before he finds another wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a real paid local opening with enough after-fare weekly pay would help.
